Paw
pâ
n. (the foot of a beast of prey; the deliverance David reckoned on before Goliath)
From Old French poue, a paw. In 1 Samuel 17 the Hebrew is simply yad, hand — the lion's hand and the bear's hand, set in the same sentence as the hand of the Philistine, so that the three are weighed as one kind of danger.

Biblical Definition

David's argument before Saul is not about his own ability, and it is not a boast about the past: “David said moreover, The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the LORD be with thee” (1 Samuel 17:37). The Hebrew word is the same for all three — the lion's hand, the bear's hand, the Philistine's hand — so the reasoning is an argument from experience about who does the delivering, not an estimate of the odds. The ground of his confidence is stated in the previous verse and it is theological, not martial: “Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God” (1 Samuel 17:36). Elsewhere the beasts close in with no deliverance in sight, and the Psalm that says so is the Psalm of the cross: “For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 22:16). Daniel's vision uses the claw for empire itself: “whose teeth were of iron, and his nails of brass; which devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet” (Daniel 7:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a paw as the foot of a beast of prey having claws, as the lion, the tiger, the dog, the cat — and the verb, to scrape with the fore foot.

expand to see more

PAW, n. [W. pawen.] The foot of a beast of prey having claws, as the lion, the tiger, the dog, the cat, &c.

PAW, v.i. To draw the fore foot along the ground; to scrape with the fore foot.

PAW, v.t. To handle roughly; to scratch; to flatter.

CLAW, n. The sharp hooked nail of a beast, bird or other animal.

DELIVER, v.t. [L. libero.] To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue from danger.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 17:37 — "David said moreover, The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the LORD be with thee."

1 Samuel 17:36 — "Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God."

Psalm 22:16 — "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet."

Daniel 7:19 — "Then I would know the truth of the fourth beast, which was diverse from all the others, exceeding dreadful, whose teeth were of iron, and his nails of brass; which devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet;"

Modern Corruption

David and Goliath is preached as a lesson in self-belief, with the giant recast as whatever obstacle a hearer faces and David as the hearer.

expand to see more

The motivational reading puts the listener in David's place and makes the story about courage. Verse 36 forbids it. David's stated reason for expecting to win is not that he is brave or skilled but that this Philistine hath defied the armies of the living God — the fight is God's, and David is the one God happens to be using. The lion and the bear are evidence in an argument about the LORD's record, not about David's. A sermon that swaps the subject of the sentence has told the opposite story with the same props.

Psalm 22:16 keeps the reading honest in the other direction, and it is the verse the triumphal version cannot use. There the beasts encircle and no deliverance comes; the hands and feet are pierced. Scripture's Shepherd-King was delivered out of the paw of the lion, and Scripture's greater Son was not — because He was the offering. Any doctrine promising the believer David's outcome in every trial has to explain Psalm 22, and the explanation is that the Son endured the beasts so that His people could be raised out of them at the last.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yad (H3027), hand, paw; ari (H738), a lion; dob (H1677), a bear; Aramaic tephar (H2953), a nail, claw.

expand to see more

Hebrew yad (H3027) — hand; used of the lion, the bear, and the Philistine alike in 1 Samuel 17:37.

Hebrew ari (H738) — a lion; 1 Peter 5:8 keeps the figure for the adversary.

Hebrew dob (H1677) — a bear; the second of David's witnesses.

Hebrew keleb (H3611) — a dog; Psalm 22:16, the pack that compassed the Sufferer.

Aramaic tephar (H2953) — nail, claw; Daniel 7:19, the fourth beast's nails of brass.

Usage

"“Out of the paw of the lion” — evidence about the LORD, not about David."

"“He hath defied the armies of the living God” — whose quarrel it actually is."

"“Dogs have compassed me” — the encirclement with no rescue."
